title: TIM: A Sensitive-Parameter-Privacy Blind Watermarking Based on Zero-Knowledge Proof
authors: Haoran Si, Xi Lin, and Huiyan Chen
abstract:
Blind watermarking enables image ownership verification without requiring the original image. However, existing schemes usually require the owner to reveal the watermark seed and watermark positions during extraction. This creates a strong trust assumption on the verifier. Once such secrets are exposed, a malicious verifier can forge or remove the watermark. In this paper, we present TIM, the first publicly verifiable blind watermarking scheme with sensitive parameters privacy based on zero-knowledge proof. TIM reconstructs the extraction procedure of Integer DCT blind watermarking into an arithmetic-circuit-friendly form. This allows the owner to prove correct extraction without revealing the watermark seed or embedding positions.

TIM addresses three main challenges.
The first is the high proving cost for high-resolution images.  The second is the conflict between circuit rigidity and watermark robustness. The third is the hashing overhead of iterative state binding.
To address them, TIM combines Nova and Spartan to decompose full-image extraction into iterative proofs. It uses a threshold-based voting mechanism for robust detection. It also introduces a hierarchical state update mechanism to reduce circuit and memory costs. Experiments show that TIM preserves good imperceptibility and robustness while achieving practical efficiency. For a 4K image, proof generation takes 5.61 minutes and uses 9.61 GB peak memory. These results show that TIM is the first blind watermarking scheme to achieve seed privacy, public verifiability, and practical performance for high-resolution image ownership proofs.

1    Introduction
With the rapid proliferation of social platforms and generative media, digital images are pro-
duced and redistributed at unprecedented scale, making provenance and ownership attribu-
tion an increasingly important problem. Blind watermarkings possess an inherent advantage
in practical deployments because watermark extraction can be performed without access to
the original image, and classical watermarking designs have studied this goal across spread-
spectrum [1], QIM [2], DCT-domain [3, 4], SVD-based [5], and hybrid spatial-frequency

                                                1
constructions [6]. However, existing blind watermarkings still require the image owner to
disclose the watermark seed to the verifier during the extraction phase, where the seed de-
termines the embedding information of the watermark values. This extraction mechanism
implicitly relies on a critical security assumption: the verifier must be trusted. With the
seed, an untrusted verifier can readily remove the watermark from the image, or forge wa-
termarked images associated with this seed, thereby jeopardizing the copyright interests of
the image owner.
    In recent years, AI-based watermarkings [7] enable verification without requiring the dis-
closure of a seed, and have attracted considerable attention. However, their training datasets
may be subject to poisoning attacks [8], and models may be vulnerable to adversarial manip-
ulations, resulting in non-deterministic detection outcomes. Consequently, such approaches
are unable to provide mathematically auditable security guarantees. Therefore, there remains
a lack of a mathematically auditable watermarking scheme capable of effectively protecting
the watermark seed and other sensitive information.
    Zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) [9, 10] is a cryptographic primitive that enables a prover to
convince a verifier of a statement without revealing the underlying secret witness, making
it a natural foundation for privacy-preserving ownership verification. This property makes
ZKPs inherently well suited for privacy-preserving image ownership verification scenarios,
and non-interactive proof systems commonly rely on the Fiat–Shamir paradigm [11] to sup-
port public verification. Recent systems have explored ZKPs for attested images [12] and
image-transformation verification [13, 14], showing that arithmetic-circuit proofs can pro-
vide auditable guarantees for visual media. A naive approach is that, takes the watermark
seed and embedding locations as secret witnesses, with the watermark values derived from
the seed. The watermarked image and extraction parameters are then provided as public
inputs, and an arithmetic circuit is constructed to compile the entire watermark extraction
procedure. Using the ZKPs, the image owner can subsequently convince the verifier of the
validity of the extraction result without revealing the underlying secret witnesses. Moreover,
due to the soundness of ZKPs, malicious prover that does not possess the correct seed cannot
forge a valid proof.
    It seems that ZKP simultaneously preserves the privacy of the watermark seed and en-
ables publicly verifiable proof of ownership. However, this naive approach faces two funda-
mental challenges in practice.
    The first challenge concerns computational performance. Modern high-resolution images,
such as 4K (3840 × 2160) and 8K (7680 × 4320) images, contain an enormous number of
pixels. Compiling the complete watermark extraction process for an entire image into a single
arithmetic circuit would result in a constraint system whose scale far exceeds the practical
capabilities of existing ZKPs. VerITAS [13] has demonstrated that proving an 8K image
editing workflow using PLONK2 [15] requires nearly 130 GB of memory, such approaches
impose substantial hardware requirements in practical applications.
    The second challenge concerns robustness. Arithmetic circuits are inherently static and
rigid, every constraint encoded in the circuit must be satisfied exactly. However, the robust-
ness of blind watermarking requires that, the extraction algorithm be capable of recovering
a sufficient watermark values even the watermarked image has undergone reasonable mod-
ifications, such as compression or minor editing, a requirement widely studied in robust
spread-spectrum [1], QIM [2], and DCT-domain watermarking [3, 4]. Directly compile a

                                              2
zero-error watermark extraction requirement into the circuit constraints implies that the en-
tire proof becomes invalid even if only a single pixel of the image has been modified. There
exists a fundamental tension between the rigidity of ZKPs and the robustness requirements
of watermarking schemes.
    Accordingly, we propose the central question addressed in this work:
    Can we construct a blind watermarking scheme based on ZKP such that simultaneously
preserves the privacy of the watermark seed and embedding locations, achieves a reasonable
degree of robustness, and maintains practical efficiency?
    To address the aforementioned question, we propose TIM (This Image Is Mine), the first
blind watermarking scheme designed to reconcile privacy, robustness, and practical efficiency.
In a high level, TIM adopts an Integer Discrete Cosine Transform (Integer DCT) watermark-
ing, following the integer-transform design of H.264/AVC [16, 17] and prior integer-DCT
watermarking systems [18]. TIM fully reconstructs its extraction algorithm as an arithmetic
circuit, thereby enabling lossless watermark extraction over finite fields. To overcome the per-
formance limit associated with a single large-scale circuit, TIM incorporates an Incremental
Verifiable Computation (IVC) framework [19], decomposing the watermark extraction pro-
cess for an entire image into a large number of fine-grained iterative steps. In each iteration,
TIM processes a single row of 4 × 4 pixel blocks and incrementally accumulates proofs of
computational correctness through the folding mechanism of Nova [20]. The Integer DCT
inherently operates on a block-based structure, this decomposition strategy aligns naturally
with the iterative paradigm of IVC. In the final stage, Spartan [21] compresses all inter-
mediate folded proofs into a succinct non-interactive zero-knowledge (zk-SNARK) proof,
following the broader line of PCP [22], IOP [23], and transparent proof-system techniques,
enabling efficient public verification.
    About robustness, TIM abandons the exact satisfaction of all constraints and instead
introduces a voting mechanism. For each watermark-embedded image block, the circuit
does not require the extracted result to be strictly identical to the expected watermark bit.
Instead, the circuit contains a extract threshold. If the difference between the extracted
coefficients of the current block falls within the prescribed threshold range, the block is
counted as a valid vote; otherwise, it is counted as an invalid vote. The out-of-circuit
verifier determines ownership based on the watermark error rate, which is defined as the
ratio of invalid votes to the total number of watermarked blocks. While the ZKP guarantees
only the correctness of the underlying computation and the reported voting results. The
voting mechanism transforms fuzzy tolerance within arithmetic circuits, into a computable
statistical decision process. This design follows the same high-level intuition as redundancy-
and threshold-based watermark detection [1, 2, 6], where ownership is decided from aggregate
evidence rather than a single exact coefficient comparison. It preserves the deterministic
nature of circuit constraints while endowing TIM with robustness against signal-processing
operations such as image compression.
    About effciency, TIM requires that the input pixels in each iteration be binded into the
hash state. For a 4K image, each iteration would involve more than 15000 hash operations,
which is a substantial pressure for a circuit. To address this, TIM introduces a hierarchical
state update mechanism based on random linear combinations. Under this mechanism, the
pixels within each block are packed into a single field element through a cascaded encoding
process, thereby reducing 16× hash operations. Then, g blocks are aggregated into a single

                                               3
digest value, and incorporated into the single hash, reduces g× hash operations. The security
of this mechanism is guaranteed by the Schwartz-Zippel lemma [24].
    In summary, the contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

    • We propose TIM, the first blind watermarking based on zero-knowledge proofs that
      provides seed-privacy. TIM fully compiles the extraction algorithm of an Integer DCT
      watermarking into an arithmetic circuit, enabling publicly verifiable image ownership
      proofs without revealing the watermark seed or embedding locations. It fundamentally
      eliminates the risks of watermark removal and forgery arising from seed disclosure.

    • We systematically address the three challenges of privacy, robustness, and practicality.
      TIM incorporates the watermark seed and index as witnesses within the ZKP relation,
      leveraging the zero-knowledge to provide privacy. TIM provides redundancy for water-
      mark extraction through voting mechanism, without compromising the determinism of
      the arithmetic circuit. With respect to practicality, TIM leverages IVC to decompose
      a large-scale circuit into a sequence of constant-size step circuits, and introduces the
      hierarchical state update mechanism, thereby enabling scalable proof generation for
      high-resolution images.

    • We conduct extensive experiments on a range of standard resolutions images. The
      robustness evaluation shows that, under JPEG compression with a quality factor of
      QF = 70, TIM achieves a 480P watermark extraction error rate of 4.49%. The per-
      formance evaluation shows that, for a 4K image, TIM requires 5.61 minutes for proof
      generation, while verification takes only approximately 0.73 seconds. The experimen-
      tal results demonstrate that TIM is the first blind watermarking scheme to achieve
      publicly verifiable watermark ownership verification with seed privacy protection at a
      practically efficient scale.


2     Related Work
Blind watermarking. Classical blind watermarking schemes including spread spectrum
watermarking [1], Quantization Index Modulation (QIM) [2], and various DCT- and DWT-
domain approaches [3–5]. All of them require the verifier to obtain the watermark seed
during the extraction phase. Consequently, disclosure of the seed directly enables watermark
removal or forgery, the verifier must be trusted.
    ZKPs and multimedia verification. The application of zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs)
[9] to multimedia content verification has emerged as a promising research direction in recent
years. VerITAS [13] applies PLONK2 to the verification of 8K image editing workflows.
However, its monolithic large-scale circuit requires nearly 130 GB of memory, imposing
substantial hardware demands and limiting its practical deployability. VIMz [14] further
advances this research by IVC to realize arithmetic circuit representations of image editing
operations.
    Incremental verifiable computation. Incremental Verifiable Computation (IVC)
[20, 25, 26] decomposes a long computation into a large number of uniform short steps,



                                              4
which are subsequently compressed into a succinct proof through iterations. Nova [20] com-
bines the R1CS instances generated at each step into a single relaxed R1CS instance, thereby
avoiding the expensive pairing operations typically required in recursive SNARK construc-
tions. Building upon Nova, Spartan [21] further provides zero-knowledge guarantees and
proof succinctness. TIM does not require non-uniform IVC as employed by SuperNova [25],
nor does it rely on the custom gates introduced in HyperNova [26].
    Integer DCT. The floating-point coefficients used in the standard DCT prevent it from
being represented exactly within finite-field arithmetic circuits. The Integer DCT introduced
in H.264/AVC [16] replaces the floating-point DCT with an integer-kernel approximation,
allowing all computations to be mapped lossless into addition and multiplication constraints
over a finite field. Integer DCT watermarking schemes [6] have been extensively validated
with respect to robustness; however, no prior work has integrated such schemes with ZKPs.

Then we review integer-based DCT watermarking [27], zk-SNARKs [9] and their circuit

TIM’s efficiency. These preliminaries establish the formal foundation needed to describe

3.1     Integer DCT Watermarking
TIM adopts the 4 × 4 integer discrete cosine transform (DCT) used by prior integer-DCT
watermarking [18] and defined in the H.264 video coding standard [16, 17]. This transform
maps a 4 × 4 pixel block to the frequency domain using a separable butterfly structure whose
matrix consists entirely of small integer coefficients like {1, 2}. For a one-dimensional input

The 2D transform is obtained by applying this 1D butterfly row-wise, followed by the same

inverse DCT recovers the original pixels exactly via the reverse lifting procedure, with no
floating-point error.
    In the frequency domain, each 4 × 4 block yields 16 DCT coefficients arranged from low
frequency (top-left) to high frequency (bottom-right). To balance imperceptibility against
robustness, the watermark is embedded in the mid-frequency region. Specifically, for each
selected block, let mid-frequency coefficients a = Y [1][2] and b = Y [2][1] is retrieved, and the
expected watermark bit can be inferred from the sign of a − b. When the watermarked image
has undergone lossy processing such as JPEG compression, the coefficients are perturbed by
quantization noise, and a decision threshold, is used to distinguish valid embedded signals
from noise, following the standard robustness intuition of transform-domain watermarking
[3, 4, 6].
    A key challenge in realizing this transform inside an arithmetic circuit is that the division-
by-two operations must respect integer truncation semantics rather than modular inversion
over Fp .

3.3    Incrementally Verifiable Computation
Proving watermark extraction over a high-resolution image involves processing thousands of
blocks—far beyond what a single flat circuit can accommodate. TIM addresses this through

and produces, alongside the final state zT , a proof ΠT that accumulates the correctness of

    TIM instantiates IVC using Nova [20], a recursive proof system based on folding. At
each step, Nova folds the current running proof with the new step claim into a single relaxed
R1CS instance of size O(|F|), where F is the number of constraints in the step circuit. This
avoids expensive recursion overhead and does not require a trusted setup.
    However, Nova does not guarantee zero-knowledge or produce a succinct final proof suit-
able for non-interactive verification. To obtain a full zk-SNARK, TIM wraps Nova’s accumu-
lated relation inside Spartan [21], a transparent proof system that adds the zero-knowledge
and succinctness guarantees missing from the base iteration protocol. Spartan masks wit-
ness information through random linear combinations and enables the verifier to check only
a small number of polynomial evaluations. The combined Nova+Spartan construction thus
inherits Nova’s efficient incremental proving while satisfying all four zk-SNARK properties
of §3.2.

3.4    ZK-Friendly Hash Function
Standard hash functions such as SHA-256 [30] rely on bit-wise Boolean operations that trans-
late to tens of thousands of constraints when arithmetized over a prime field. Poseidon [31] is
a ZK-friendly hash function designed to operate natively over Fp via a sponge construction.
A single Poseidon permutation consumes only a few hundred R1CS constraints, making it
several orders of magnitude cheaper than SHA-256 inside a circuit.
    TIM uses Poseidon for two distinct purposes: (1) it serves as the state transition hash
within the IVC loop: each iteration updates the running state, cryptographically binding the
entire block sequence into a compact accumulator, and (2) it acts as an in-circuit pseudo-
random generator [32], ensuring that the expected watermark sequence cannot be predicted
or biased without knowledge of s.


4     The Overview of TIM
This section provides a high-level description of TIM. It can be divided into three phases: (1)
the watermark embedding phase, in which the image generator (e.g., a camera) obtains the
original image and embeds a watermark, (2) the proof phase, in which the prover executes
the arithmetic circuit implementing the watermark extraction algorithm and generates a
proof about the extracted result, and (3) the verification phase, in which the verifier checks
the validity of the proof to ensure the validity of the extraction result, and thereby ensure
the validity of image ownership.

4.2    Proof Phase
Recall that disclosure of seed s would allow anyone to generate the watermark values, while
disclosure of watermark index Iwm would reveal the watermark positions. In this phase, s
and Iwm are taken as private witness. The proof therefore attests that the prover knows
a seed and an index under which the watermarked image yields a valid extraction result,
without ever exposing either secret to the verifier.
    The arithmetic circuit is compiled from the watermark extraction algorithm. We decom-
pose the extraction algorithm into an iterative function F adapted to Nova’s IVC frame-
work. We use IVC because the extraction workload is highly repetitive and naturally block-
structured. Instead of proving one monolithic circuit for all image blocks, IVC keeps the
base circuit tied to a single row of 4 × 4 blocks, reuses the same circuit across iterations, and
folds the execution trace into a succinct final proof. This choice directly reduces peak circuit
size and makes high-resolution proving feasible, while preserving the same public verification
semantics through the final Spartan proof.
    TIM maintains four state variables updated across iterations, denoted z = (za , zb , zc , zd ),
where

   • za is a running Poseidon hash digest that binds every pixel to the computation, ensuring
     the prover commits to the entire image,

   • zb is a block counter, incremented once per traversed block,

   • zc is a watermark counter, incremented once per watermarked block (i.e., per block
     with Iwm [i] = 1),

   • zd is an error counter, incremented once per watermarked block whose extracted coef-
     ficient relationship does not match the expected watermark bit.



                                                9
    In every iteration, F performs three tasks: (1) regenerate the watermark bit sequence
from the seed s via hash function, (2) extract all blocks and evaluate the watermark decision
rule on each watermarked block, and (3) update the four states for the next iteration. The
detailed construction of F is provided in §5.
    The watermark index Iwm produced during embedding (§4.1) serves as the block selection
mask in the circuit. It only blocks with Iwm [i] = 1 contribute to zc and zd . This index is
provided as a private witness alongside the seed. A malicious prover could in principle
supply an adversarially chosen index that discards failing blocks to artificially lower the
error count. In the current design, we assume the prover is the legitimate image owner who
has no incentive to weaken its own ownership claim, this honesty assumption is consistent
like the C2PA-based trust model.

4.3    Verification Phase
In this phase, the verifier checks the Spartan proof π generated during the proof phase.
A successful verification confirms that the prover honestly executed the function F in the
arithmetic circuit and that the counters zc and zd faithfully reflect the extraction outcome.
The verifier then computes the error rate zd /zc outside the circuit. If zd /zc falls below a
pre-defined threshold (e.g., 30%), the watermarked image is considered valid, demonstrating
that the prover holds knowledge of both the seed s and the watermark index Iwm , and
therefore holds ownership of the image.


5     TIM’s Iteration Function
In this section, we present the Construction of TIM arithmetic circuit, which is compiled
from the iteration function F.
    Recall that in TIM, the iteration function F should (1) generate the watermark value wm,

6     Threat Model and Security Analysis
In TIM, the prover is the legitimate image owner, who holds the original image, the water-
mark seed s, and the watermark index indexwm produced during embedding. The verifier is
any third party who wishes to verify ownership of a watermarked image Iwm , but may behave
maliciously by attempting to recover s or indexwm from the proof. An external adversary is
a PPT entity who possesses the watermarked image but does not know s or indexwm , and
whose goal is to forge an ownership proof that passes verification.
    Both s and Iwm must remain hidden from the verifier and the adversary. Knowledge of
s allows one to regenerate the full watermark bit sequence, and thus to forge watermarked
images or to erase the watermark by inverting the embedding logic. Knowledge of the index
reveals which blocks carry watermark information, enabling targeted removal or substitution
attacks.
    The adversary and the malicious verifier have access to the watermarked image, the
proof π, and all public parameters of the proof system. We consider a single-proof setting:
the adversary cannot collect multiple proofs from the same prover to perform cross-proof
correlation analysis. The attack surface includes both cryptographic attacks seed recovery,
index recovery, proof forgery, and signal-processing attacks aimed at watermark removal via
compression, filtering, or transcoding.
    We make the following assumptions. The prover is honest and performs embedding and
proof generation faithfully, a dishonest prover gains no advantage from weakening its own
ownership claim. The embedding phase itself is trusted, relying on the C2PA provenance
chain to guarantee that the watermarked image indeed originates from the claimed prover
[36]. On the cryptographic side, we assume Poseidon is collision-resistant in the random-
oracle model [31], that Nova provides knowledge soundness for the incremental computation
[20], and that Spartan provides zero-knowledge for the final proof [21].
    TIM aims to satisfy the following properties:

    • Completeness. An honest prover who holds the correct s and indexwm always produces
      a proof that the verifier accepts.

    • Soundness. An adversary who does not know s or indexwm cannot produce a proof for
      Iwm whose accumulated error rate zd /zc falls below the verification threshold.

    • Zero-knowledge. The proof reveals no information about s or indexwm beyond what
      can be inferred from the public output and the watermarked image.

    • Succinctness. Proof size and verification time are independent of the number of image
      blocks.


                                               16
    The soundness reduces to the knowledge soundness of Nova and the collision resistance
of Poseidon [20, 31]. Any valid proof must attest to a witness (s, indexwm ) whose Poseidon
expansion. An adversary who does not possess such a seed must either find a second preimage
of the watermarked coefficient sequence under Poseidon, or forge a Nova proof without a
satisfying witness. Both are infeasible under the stated assumptions. The zero-knowledge of
the witness follows directly from the ZK property of Spartan, which ensures that the proof
leaks no witness information [9, 21]. Completeness holds trivially when the prover supplies
the correct inputs.
    Multi-proof unlinkability is not claimed. In TIM, we only guarantee zero-knowledge for
individual proofs. Attacks against the embedding phase itself (e.g., side-channel leakage of
s during injection) are outside the scope of the proof system. Signal-processing attacks that
degrade watermark detectability are evaluated experimentally rather than being addressed
via cryptographic guarantees.


7         Experiments
This section reports three experiments: watermark image quality, JPEG robustness, and
proof-system performance. We test whether TIM preserves visual fidelity, remains robust
under compression, and keeps proving and verification costs practical on standard image
resolutions.

7.1         Experimental Setup
We implemented TIM2 by compiling the extraction procedure into an arithmetic circuit using
Circom [28, 29], and then proving the row-wise iteration with Microsoft’s Nova implementa-
tion [20, 37]. The final non-interactive proof is produced by Spartan [21]. All proof-related
computations use the scalar field Fp of the Pasta elliptic curve [35], where p ≈ 2254 . Po-
seidon [31] is configured with width 3, 8 full rounds, and 57 partial rounds, matching the
in-circuit hash used both for watermark-bit generation and for state aggregation. All exper-
iments were conducted on a machine equipped with an Intel Core i9-14900K processor and
48 GB of RAM, running Ubuntu 22.04.

  7.3.2                 Verifier’s complexity
  A key advantage of TIM is that verification complexity is independent of the image resolution
  and the number of IVC iterations. The verifier invokes Spartan’s verification algorithm on the
  Spartan proof π to ensure the validity of extract result. By the succinctness of Spartan [21],
  the verification time is polylog(|C|), i.e., it grows only logarithmically with the circuit size.
  In our experiments, Spartan verification consumed approximately 0.75 s across all resolutions
  from 480P to 8K, confirming that the verification cost is essentially constant in practice.


  8                 Conclusion
  This paper presents TIM, a privacy-preserving blind-watermark ownership verification scheme
  for images. TIM enables an image owner to prove that a watermarked image was correctly


                                                                21
generated and extracted without revealing the watermark seed, watermark index, or other
private witness data. The main innovation of TIM is the integration of integer-DCT wa-
termarking with zero-knowledge proofs. We reconstruct the watermark extraction process
into an arithmetic-circuit-friendly form, use Poseidon to generate watermark bits and update
states, and employ Nova with Spartan to support scalable proof generation over standard
image resolutions. The experimental results show that TIM preserves image quality, remains
robust under JPEG compression within the tested threshold, and keeps verification efficient.
For 4K images, TIM achieves a PSNR of 46.02 dB, generates the proof in 5.61 minutes with
9.61 GB peak memory, and keeps verification at approximately 0.75 s. These results demon-
strate that privacy-preserving public verification of blind-watermark ownership is practical
for images.
    Our future work will further enhance the robustness, and extend TIM beyond still images.
In particular, TIM can be adapted to audio and video watermarking, enabling privacy-
preserving ownership verification for broader multimedia content.
